label: Gary Keller & Jay Papasan, The ONE Thing (2013)
note: Extraordinary results come from extreme focus — doing less by narrowing to the single most important task instead of spreading across many.

label: Cal Newport, Deep Work (2016)
note: The source for the 4 Rules of Deep Work and the Shutdown Ritual — the case for scheduled, undistracted focus as a rare and valuable skill worth protecting deliberately.

label: David Allen, Getting Things Done (2001)
note: The source for the 2-Minute Rule — a full system for capturing everything so your mind doesn't have to hold it.

label: Brian Tracy, Eat That Frog! (2001)
note: Do the hardest, most important task first, before anything else gets a chance to eat the day instead.

label: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (2021)
note: A corrective to productivity culture itself — you will never get everything done, and that's the actual starting point, not a problem to solve.

label: Laura Vanderkam, 168 Hours (2010)
note: Reframes "I don't have time" as a prioritization problem, not a math problem — everyone gets the same 168 hours a week.

label: Damon Zahariades, The Art of Saying No (2017)
note: Actionable steps to stop people-pleasing and protect your schedule — pairs directly with the Boundaries & Saying No group above.

label: Susan Newman, The Book of No (2005)
note: Practical scripts for turning down requests from colleagues, friends, and family.

label: James Clear, Atomic Habits (2018)
note: The source for the 4 Laws of Behavior Change and habit stacking — small, systematic changes compound into remarkably different outcomes over time.

label: Stephen Covey, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989)
note: A broader personal-effectiveness philosophy rather than habit-formation mechanics — its ideas show up scattered across this site (Begin with the End in Mind, Put First Things First) more than on this page specifically.

label: Gabriele Oettingen, Rethinking Positive Thinking (2014)
note: The research behind the WOOP Method — positive thinking alone underperforms positive thinking paired with a real obstacle and a plan.

label: Colin Powell, It Worked for Me: In Life and Leadership (2012)
note: Source of "Bad news isn't wine. It doesn't improve with age," quoted on the Status Report Template — the case for flagging at risk and off track honestly instead of letting a red status quietly age into a crisis.

label: Simon Sinek, Start with Why (2009)
note: The source for the Strategy-is-the-why framing on Product Vision & Strategy — people follow the reason behind a plan more than the plan itself.

label: Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011)
note: The sharpest explanation of why strategy is hard: most of what gets called strategy is really just a goal or vision statement in disguise. Real strategy is a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and coherent action.

label: Colin Bryar & Bill Carr, Working Backwards: Insights, Stories, and Secrets from Inside Amazon (2021)
note: Written by two former Amazon executives who helped build the process; the definitive source for the PR/FAQ method on the Working Backwards Plan section — why the press release is dated as if the product already shipped and succeeded, not written on day one.
